title: Why Granting a Favor Makes You Like People More
author: Admired Leadership Field Notes
summary: Doing a small favor for someone increases the helper's liking of the recipient, not the other way around. This counterintuitive finding (Cognitive Dissonance, Self-Perception Theory, Impression Management converge on it) inverts the common assumption. The operational claim for leaders: asking a team member for a small, thoughtful favor signals respect and invests them in the leader's success. Mentors feel more connected to those who seek their advice; team members who feel their help was needed grow more loyal to the leader. The framing shift from directive to favor is what does the work. Requests that travel well: introductions, advice on decisions, validation of ideas, edits, demonstrations. Used sparingly and sincerely, these produce affection that praise cannot manufacture. The memorable close: we do not only help people we like, we start liking the people we help.
points: People who do favors for others reorganize their beliefs to make the relationship feel worthwhile, increasing liking through Cognitive Dissonance and Self-Perception.
Leaders who ask team members for thoughtful favors (not directives) signal respect and invest those members in the leader's success.
Favor-framing activates more loyalty and connection than praise or recognition because it taps into the helper's own need to justify why they cared enough to help.
Small, sincere requests (for advice, an introduction, validation, edits) produce genuine affection that volume of praise cannot replicate.
quotes: People generally believe they must feel warmth and connection before choosing to help someone. Liking people before agreeing to help them seems like the natural order of things. But the opposite is also true.

After doing someone a favor, people begin to like the other party more, even if they felt indifferent about them beforehand. This phenomenon is often termed the Ben Franklin Effect because he wrote about using small requests to soften his political rivals.” “The logic behind this effect is straightforward. People don not generally help others they dislike, so if they agree to a small request or favor, they reason they must like them after all. The need to align our beliefs and actions is a powerful force.

Leaders like people more who ask them for their advice and seek their feedback. The leader will often feel prideful for the other person's success. This is why mentors, coaches, and leaders often feel more deeply connected and committed to those who actively seek their guidance.

Leaders who ask team members to help them in various small projects, initiatives, and tasks give them the attention they crave. The more these requests are seen as doing the leader a favor, rather than complying with a directive, the more connection team members feel.

Granting small favors helps to build rapport, trust, and likability for both leaders and team members. People feel more connected when they are asked to contribute, especially to requests that seem personal and confidential.

Thoughtful favors that signal respect and show a genuine interest in others are best, of course. Requesting an introduction, asking for advice, seeking a ride, validating an idea, requesting a check or edit, thinking through a decision, and soliciting a demonstration are common examples.
This effect flips our assumption about generosity. We don't just help people we like. We start liking the people we help.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
